title: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Network Device CLI
shortTitle: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Network Device CLI
summary: Routers, switches and firewalls expose a text command line that is the normal way to configure them, and it is also an execution path that sits outside most endpoint controls. Access arrives over a console cable, telnet, or SSH, and most platforms separate a read-only mode from a privileged mode that unlocks configuration commands. Once in privileged mode an intruder can rewrite routing and access control lists, alter the startup configuration that is loaded at boot, install or boot a tampered system image, turn off logging, and clear the local history buffers that would otherwise show the session. Several network operating systems also carry a scripting interpreter, such as an embedded Tcl engine or an event manager, which lets a saved script run further commands automatically on a timer or a trigger. The evidence lives on the device and in the systems around it: authentication and accounting records from the central login server, syslog messages describing configuration changes and interface state, startup and running configuration differences, and login records from source addresses that never normally administer infrastructure. The practical discriminator is cadence and source: a change made during a documented window from a management jump host is routine, while a configuration change from an unexpected address outside a window, or a session that ends with logging disabled, is not.

beginner.definition: Network devices such as routers, switches and firewalls have their own command line. It is a text screen where an administrator types commands. This technique is about attackers using that same text screen to run their own commands.
beginner.whyItMatters: Network devices often sit outside normal endpoint protection. Many of them keep few logs, or send logs to a server nobody reads. Someone with this command line access can redirect traffic, change passwords and switch off logging. If you never check these devices, you may not notice an intrusion at all.
howItWorks: An attacker reaches the device through a console cable, telnet, or SSH.
They sign in with a weak, default, or stolen administrator password.
They enter a privileged mode that unlocks the configuration commands.
Commands change routing, access lists, or the startup file loaded at boot.
Some devices include a scripting interpreter that can run a saved command program.
The attacker may disable logging or clear buffers so the session leaves no trace.
beginner.example: Think of a large building. The lights, lifts and door locks are controlled from one small panel in the basement. Staff use the panel every day, so nobody watches it closely. An intruder who finds the panel can unlock doors, stop the cameras and change which floor the lifts stop at. A network device command line is that panel. It is powerful, rarely watched, and often still protected by the simple password it shipped with.
takeaways: A network device is a computer, so treat its login like an administrator login.
Central login and accounting records are the best evidence of who changed what.
Compare the running configuration to the startup configuration to spot quiet edits.

objectives: Explain what a network device command line is and how administrators reach it.
Describe the difference between read-only and privileged command modes on such devices.
List the kinds of change an intruder can make through the device command line.
Name the log sources that reveal device logins and configuration changes.
Explain how a device scripting interpreter extends the command set beyond typed commands.
